def: A pathogen is a disease-causing organism; different pathogens (protozoa, bacteria, virus) cause diseases like malaria, typhoid and AIDS through different modes of transmission.
points: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium (a protozoan), transmitted by the bite of female Anopheles mosquito.
Plasmodium multiplies inside red blood cells and causes cyclical fever with chills, due to rupture of RBCs releasing toxins.
Typhoid is caused by the bacterium Salmonella typhi, spread through contaminated food and water.
Typhoid symptoms include sustained high fever, weakness, abdominal pain and headache.
AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome) is caused by HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus), which attacks helper T-lymphocytes, weakening immunity.
HIV spreads through unprotected sex, blood transfusion with infected blood, sharing needles, or from mother to child.
Because immunity is destroyed, AIDS patients die from other infections (opportunistic infections), not HIV itself.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Plasmodium in Anopheles bite"] --> B["Enters RBC and multiplies"]
  B --> C["RBC ruptures releasing toxins"]
  C --> D["Cyclical fever with chills"]

example: The Widal test is used to confirm typhoid by detecting antibodies against Salmonella typhi in the patient's blood.
tip: For each disease, write: causative agent, mode of transmission, and one key symptom — this three-point pattern matches most board answers.

def: Immunity is the body's ability to resist pathogens; it is of two broad types — innate (present from birth, non-specific) and acquired (develops after exposure, specific).
points: Innate immunity includes physical barriers (skin, mucus), physiological barriers (acid in stomach), and cellular barriers (WBCs like neutrophils, macrophages).
Innate immunity acts immediately but is not specific to a particular pathogen.
Acquired immunity is specific and has memory — it recognises a pathogen it has met before and responds faster the second time.
Acquired immunity is of two types: humoral (B-lymphocytes producing antibodies) and cell-mediated (T-lymphocytes destroying infected cells).
Active immunity develops when the body itself produces antibodies (after infection or vaccination).
Passive immunity is when ready-made antibodies are given directly (e.g., through mother's milk or injection).

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Immunity"] --> B["Innate: skin, mucus, WBCs"]
  A --> C["Acquired: specific and has memory"]
  C --> D["Humoral: B cells make antibodies"]
  C --> E["Cell mediated: T cells kill infected cells"]

example: A baby gets passive immunity from antibodies in mother's milk (colostrum), protecting it until its own immune system matures.
tip: Draw the branching chart of immunity types — examiners award marks for correctly classifying innate vs acquired, active vs passive.

def: Vaccination is the process of introducing a weakened, killed or inactivated form of a pathogen (or its antigen) into the body to stimulate the immune system to produce memory cells, giving protection against future infection.
points: A vaccine contains antigens that trigger the immune system without causing the actual disease.
The body produces antibodies and memory B and T cells in response.
On future exposure to the real pathogen, memory cells respond rapidly and strongly, preventing disease.
This principle is called immunological memory, the basis of all vaccination programs.
Examples of vaccines: BCG (for tuberculosis), OPV (oral polio vaccine), DPT (diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus).
Mass vaccination can eliminate a disease from a population, as achieved with smallpox.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Vaccine with antigen given"] --> B["Immune system makes antibodies"]
  B --> C["Memory cells form"]
  C --> D["Faster response on real infection"]

example: Smallpox was completely eradicated worldwide through a global vaccination campaign, showing the power of immunization.
tip: Explain the term 'memory cells' clearly — this is the key scientific concept examiners check for in vaccination questions.

def: Cancer is a disease in which cells divide uncontrollably and abnormally, invading and damaging surrounding tissues, caused by mutations in genes that control cell growth.
points: Normal cells follow controlled cell division; cancer cells lose this control and divide continuously.
Agents causing cancer are called carcinogens — they can be physical (radiation), chemical (tobacco, certain dyes), or biological (some viruses).
Proto-oncogenes are normal genes that, when mutated, become oncogenes and promote cancer.
Tumour suppressor genes normally stop abnormal division; their loss also leads to cancer.
A benign tumour stays localized; a malignant tumour invades other tissues and can spread (metastasis).
Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells from the original site to other parts of the body via blood or lymph.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Carcinogen exposure"] --> B["Mutation in genes"]
  B --> C["Uncontrolled cell division"]
  C --> D["Tumour formation"]
  D --> E["Metastasis to other organs"]

example: Prolonged tobacco chewing is a major cause of oral cancer, acting as a chemical carcinogen damaging mouth tissue cells.
tip: Clearly differentiate benign from malignant tumour — this comparison is a favourite 2-mark question.

def: Drug and alcohol abuse is the habitual, excessive use of substances like narcotics, alcohol or tobacco that harm physical and mental health and can cause addiction and dependence.
points: Addiction is a psychological attachment to a substance for its pleasurable effects.
Dependence means the body needs the substance to function normally; stopping causes withdrawal symptoms.
Common abused substances: opioids (heroin, morphine), cannabinoids (marijuana), and alcohol.
Alcohol abuse damages the liver (causing cirrhosis) and impairs judgement and coordination.
Tobacco use (smoking) causes lung cancer, bronchitis and cardiovascular disease due to nicotine and tar.
Peer pressure, curiosity and stress are common reasons adolescents start substance abuse.
Awareness, counselling, family support and avoiding peer pressure help in prevention.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Curiosity or peer pressure"] --> B["Substance use begins"]
  B --> C["Tolerance develops"]
  C --> D["Addiction and dependence"]
  D --> E["Health damage: liver, lungs, brain"]

example: Chronic alcohol abuse leads to cirrhosis of the liver, where liver tissue is permanently scarred and loses normal function.
tip: Mention at least one prevention measure (counselling, family support, avoiding peer pressure) — value-based points earn extra marks.

def: Immune system disorders occur when the immune system either fails to work properly, overreacts, or attacks the body's own cells, leading to conditions like allergies, autoimmune disease, and immunodeficiency.
points: Allergy is an exaggerated immune response to otherwise harmless substances (allergens) like dust or pollen.
In allergy, IgE antibodies trigger release of histamine from mast cells, causing symptoms like sneezing, itching or swelling.
Autoimmune disorders occur when the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own cells, as in rheumatoid arthritis.
Immunodeficiency disorders occur when the immune system is weak or absent, making the person prone to infections.
AIDS is an example of an acquired immunodeficiency disorder, caused by HIV destroying helper T-cells.
Some immunodeficiencies are inherited (congenital), present from birth.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Immune disorders"] --> B["Allergy: overreaction to allergen"]
  A --> C["Autoimmune: attacks own cells"]
  A --> D["Immunodeficiency: weak immune response"]

example: In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system attacks the joints' own tissue, causing inflammation, pain and stiffness.
tip: Give one example disorder under each category (allergy, autoimmune, immunodeficiency) for a complete, well-structured answer.
